content: 1. It is essential to test the following in various settings: case definitions for uncomplicated severe acute malnutrition (SAM) in infants under 6 months of age, and different outpatient-based care packages for these infants. 2. Infants under 6 months with SAM may have underlying conditions such as complex congenital heart disease or metabolic disorders, which can be fatal if untreated. Even in developed countries, these conditions present significant diagnostic and management challenges. 3. Conditions like tuberculosis (TB), HIV, malignancies, and burns can also contribute to SAM in infants under 6 months. Addressing breastfeeding problems alone will not resolve all cases of SAM in this age group, as secondary causes must also be considered. 4. In resource-limited settings, priority issues for intervention include identifying and treating HIV in infants under 6 months. Guidelines should explicitly reference the WHO 2010 guidelines for HIV diagnosis and treatment in infants and children. 5. It is strongly recommended that all infants with unknown or uncertain HIV exposure seen in healthcare facilities have their HIV exposure status determined. This ensures that infants whose mothers were not tested during pregnancy or delivery can still benefit from counseling and treatment to prevent breast milk transmission of HIV. 6. All infants known to be exposed to HIV should be tested at 4–6 weeks using virological assays to determine their infection status. Early identification of infected infants allows access to life-saving treatment. 7. Antiretroviral therapy (ART) should be initiated in all HIV-infected infants diagnosed in the first year of life, regardless of CD4 count or clinical condition. This recommendation has been in place since 2008 but requires better implementation due to its significant impact on reducing mortality. 8. SAM treatment programs provide an important entry point for HIV treatment programs for both infants and their families. Linking SAM and HIV services can create synergies and improve outcomes for both conditions. 9. Virological testing is necessary for definitive HIV diagnosis in infants under 6 months, but this may not be universally available. Settings relying solely on antibody tests risk false-positive results in this age group. 10. Chronic diseases and disabilities, such as congenital heart disease or cerebral palsy, may underlie or contribute to SAM in infants under 6 months. These conditions should be identified and referred for appropriate treatment, even in resource-limited settings. 11. Social stigma and misunderstanding around conditions like TB, disability, and chronic diseases can hinder screening and diagnosis. These processes should be managed sensitively to mitigate stigma. 12. Catching up on routine immunizations should be a standard part of pre-discharge care for infants under 6 months with SAM. Immunization programs are based on strong evidence of mortality and morbidity benefits. 13. Infants with SAM are more vulnerable and may benefit significantly from full compliance with routine immunizations. Screening for SAM during routine immunizations could also be beneficial. 14. Breastfeeding mothers of infants with SAM should consume at least 2 liters of water daily and a diet of 2500 kcal/day. Programs should ensure mothers are educated on these needs or provided with the necessary resources. 15. Psychosocial support for caregivers of infants with SAM should be emphasized as part of the treatment package. Maternal mental health is closely linked to infant growth and outcomes. 16. Strategies offering psychosocial support must be culturally sensitive and consider local ways of expressing and addressing mental health issues. 17. Positive staff attitudes toward caregivers and greater sensitivity to mental health issues cost nothing but can significantly improve outcomes for both mothers and infants.
